text: Scheduled tasks are one of the oldest privilege-escalation paths on Linux, because they so often run as root. This lesson covers real crontab syntax, systemd timers as the modern alternative, and the actual security risk a world-writable scheduled script creates — plus the one chmod that closes it.

crontab -e opens your own personal crontab — five fields, minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, then the command. A star means every unit, so */15 in the minute field means every 15 minutes. Jobs in your own crontab run as you; system-wide jobs in /etc/crontab or /etc/cron.d/ carry one extra field naming the user to run as, since there's no single personal owner there.

A systemd timer pairs a .timer unit with a same-named .service unit. OnCalendar sets the schedule in a more readable form than cron's five fields, and Persistent=true catches up a run that was missed because the machine was off — something plain cron simply can't do. systemctl enable --now turns it on; systemctl list-timers shows every timer on the box and its next run in one place.

Timers log through journalctl, right alongside every other systemd-managed service, instead of cron's separate mail-based logging. That centralized logging and the catch-up behavior are real reasons timers have become the modern default on most current distros, even though cron still works fine and still runs on plenty of production servers today.

-rwxrwxrwx root root on a script that root's crontab calls every night means any unprivileged user on the box can edit that script, and root will execute whatever they wrote the next time it fires — a direct privilege-escalation path, not a theoretical one. The fix is chmod 750 or 700: owned by root, writable only by root, with the containing directory locked down the same way.

That's the real security read on scheduled tasks: who runs them, and who can write to what they run. Next up starts Chapter 5 — SELinux and AppArmor, the mandatory access control systems that limit what a process can do even if its permissions say it's allowed.
